slides.title: Normal Anatomy & Physiology
slides.subtitle: System of Focus: Multi-System / Environmental Health

blocks.heading: Key Concepts
blocks.html:
• Vector-borne diseases transmitted by mosquitoes, ticks, fleas
  • Aedes aegypti: dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever - daytime biter
  • Anopheles: malaria - nighttime biter
  • Climate change expanding vector habitats globally
  • Caribbean: dengue endemic; malaria eliminated from most islands; leptospirosis risk after flooding
  • Rodents transmit leptospirosis, hantavirus

blocks.heading: Normal Values
blocks.html:
• Dengue incubation: 4-10 days
  • Malaria incubation: 7-30 days (P. falciparum shorter)
  • Platelets in dengue: often <100,000 (thrombocytopenia)
  • Hematocrit in dengue: rises >20% = plasma leakage (critical phase)

blocks.heading: What the Nurse Must Know
blocks.html:
• Dengue: NO aspirin/NSAIDs (bleeding risk) - use acetaminophen for fever
  • Malaria: falciparum can be fatal within 24-48 hours if untreated
  • Dengue warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, rising HCT with falling platelets
  • Leptospirosis: harvest fever in agricultural workers, contact with rat urine-contaminated water

blocks.heading: NORMAL FUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Intact skin/mucosa barriers
  • Normal immune response to pathogens
  • No vector exposure or effective prevention
  • Normal fluid and electrolyte balance

blocks.heading: DYSFUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Viral infection: dengue virus enters via mosquito, replicates in monocytes
  • Parasitic infection: Plasmodium sporozoites enter liver, then RBCs
  • Bacterial infection: Leptospira enters through broken skin/mucosa
  • Endothelial dysfunction: capillary leakage (dengue), hemolysis (malaria)
  • Organ involvement: liver, kidney, CNS

blocks.heading: ⚠ Risk Factors (Non-Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Living in/traveling to endemic areas
  • Genetic factors (dengue: HLA types)
  • Age extremes (severe dengue more common in children and elderly)

blocks.heading: 💡 Risk Factors (Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Mosquito bites (stagnant water breeding sites)
  • No vector control measures
  • Agricultural/occupational water exposure (leptospirosis)
  • Flood exposure
  • Poor sanitation and waste management
  • No vaccination/prophylaxis

blocks.heading: 🔥 Complications
blocks.html: Dengue: plasma leakage, shock, severe bleeding, organ impairment • Malaria: cerebral malaria, severe anemia, AKI, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia • Leptospirosis: Weil disease (jaundice + renal failure), pulmonary hemorrhage • Chikungunya: chronic arthralgia (months to years) • Zika: microcephaly (congenital), Guillain-Barre syndrome
NRG Opposite: Vector/pathogen exposure leads to infection, endothelial/organ damage, bleeding/shock/organ failure

1. Vector bite or environmental exposure introduces pathogen

2. Local replication and spread to bloodstream

3. Systemic infection triggers inflammatory response

4. Endothelial/cellular damage: capillary leakage, hemolysis, organ injury

5. Host immune response: antibody-dependent enhancement (dengue), cytokine storm

6. Recovery or progression to severe disease

blocks.heading: Key Detail
blocks.html: Dengue: 4 serotypes (DENV 1-4). Secondary infection with different serotype = antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) leading to severe dengue. Malaria: P. falciparum (most severe), P. vivax/ovale (relapse from hypnozoites), P. malariae (nephrotic syndrome). Leptospira interrogans: spirochete in rodent urine, enters through mucosa/broken skin.

blocks.heading: Clinical Result
blocks.html: Dengue: febrile phase to critical phase (defervescence days 3-7: plasma leakage, bleeding) to recovery. Warning signs appear during defervescence. Malaria: RBC hemolysis leads to anemia, hemoglobinuria (blackwater fever), cerebral sequestration. Leptospirosis: biphasic - septicemic phase (fever, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion) to immune phase (meningitis, Weil disease, pulmonary hemorrhage).
NRG Sequencing: Each step leads to the next — understand the cascade to predict S/S and management

blocks.heading: Early / Mild
blocks.html:
• Dengue: sudden high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, rash
  • Malaria: fever paroxysms (chills, fever, sweating every 48-72h), headache, myalgia
  • Leptospirosis: fever, severe myalgia (calves), headache, conjunctival suffusion
  • Chikungunya: fever, severe joint pain (symmetric, debilitating)
  • Zika: low-grade fever, maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, arthralgia

blocks.heading: Severe
blocks.html:
• Dengue: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly
  • Malaria: altered consciousness (cerebral malaria), severe anemia, jaundice, dark urine
  • Leptospirosis: jaundice, oliguria, pulmonary hemorrhage
  • Chikungunya: chronic debilitating arthralgia
  • Zika: Guillain-Barre syndrome ascending paralysis

blocks.heading: Dengue shock syndrome: narrow pulse pressure, cold clammy skin, tachycardia
blocks.html:
• Dengue shock syndrome: narrow pulse pressure, cold clammy skin, tachycardia
  • Cerebral malaria: seizures, coma
  • Weil disease: jaundice + acute renal failure
  • Severe pulmonary hemorrhage (leptospirosis)
  • THIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY

blocks.heading: Diagnostic / Assessment Findings
blocks.html:
• Dengue NS1 antigen (days 1-5), IgM/IgG serology
  • Malaria: thick and thin blood smear (gold standard), RDT
  • Leptospirosis: MAT (microscopic agglutination test), PCR
  • CBC: thrombocytopenia (dengue), anemia (malaria)
  • LFTs: elevated transaminases
  • Creatinine: renal involvement

blocks.heading: Link Patho to S/S
blocks.html:
Dengue fever → Fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia (breakbone fever)

Plasma leakage → Rising HCT, falling platelets, pleural effusion, ascites

Malaria hemolysis → Anemia, jaundice, dark urine, splenomegaly

Leptospirosis Weil → Jaundice + renal failure + hemorrhage

blocks.heading: Cardiovascular
blocks.html:
• BP, HR (tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure = shock)
  • Capillary refill, skin temp
  • Signs of bleeding (petechiae, ecchymoses, mucosal)

blocks.heading: Respiratory
blocks.html:
• RR, SpO2 (pleural effusion, pulmonary hemorrhage)
  • Cough, hemoptysis
  • Work of breathing

blocks.heading: Neurological
blocks.html:
• Mental status (cerebral malaria, leptospirosis meningitis)
  • Headache severity
  • Seizure activity

blocks.heading: Key Laboratory & Diagnostic Tests
rows: >20% rise from baseline = dengue plasma leakage
Elevated in severe dengue, leptospirosis, malaria
Thick/thin smear = gold standard; RDT for rapid screening

blocks.heading: Priority Actions
blocks.html: Dengue: daily CBC and HCT monitoring (critical phase days 3-7). Strict fluid management - aggressive hydration during critical phase, then careful to avoid overload. NO aspirin/NSAIDs. Malaria: identify species (falciparum vs vivax). Monitor for cerebral involvement. Leptospirosis: early antibiotics (doxycycline, penicillin) reduce severity.

blocks.heading: 💊 Pharmacology - Nursing Monitoring
rows: Fever and pain (dengue - safe with thrombocytopenia)
Dengue critical phase: plasma leakage replacement
Monitor for fluid overload - reduce when HCT falls, platelets rise
G6PD testing REQUIRED - causes hemolysis if deficient
Platelets only for active bleeding or invasive procedures

blocks.heading: Dengue Critical Phase & Malaria Species Alert
blocks.html: Dengue critical phase occurs during DEFERVESCENCE (days 3-7) - this is when plasma leakage and bleeding occur. Daily CBC/HCT essential. HCT rising >20% from baseline with falling platelets = plasma leakage. Malaria: ALWAYS identify species - P. falciparum is medical emergency; P. vivax/ovale require primaquine for radical cure (G6PD test first).

blocks.heading: Lifestyle & Patient Education
blocks.html:
• Vector control: eliminate stagnant water (breeding sites), use bed nets, repellents (DEET)
  • Dengue vaccine: available for seropositive individuals 9-45 years (Dengvaxia)
  • Malaria prophylaxis for travelers to endemic areas
  • Protective clothing during peak mosquito hours
  • Leptospirosis: protective gear for agricultural workers, rodent control
🚨 Report Immediately: Severe abdominal pain | Persistent vomiting | Mucosal bleeding | Altered consciousness | Oliguria <400 mL/day | Temperature >40C unresponsive

blocks.heading: Nursing Diagnosis
blocks.html: Deficient fluid volume related to plasma leakage secondary to dengue fever as evidenced by rising hematocrit (52%), thrombocytopenia (45,000), and narrow pulse pressure

blocks.heading: Goal / Outcome
blocks.html: Patient will maintain hemodynamic stability with adequate tissue perfusion throughout the critical phase (days 3-7).

blocks.heading: Interventions
blocks.html:
• Aggressive isotonic IV fluid resuscitation per protocol
  • Vital signs and capillary refill q1-2h
  • Daily CBC, HCT, platelet count
  • Strict I&O, daily weight
  • Monitor for bleeding (petechiae, gum bleeding, melena)
  • NO aspirin or NSAIDs - acetaminophen only

blocks.heading: Rationale
blocks.html: Plasma leakage during dengue critical phase causes hemoconcentration and hypovolemia. Isotonic fluids replace intravascular volume. HCT monitoring guides fluid therapy - rising HCT = continue fluids; falling HCT = reduce fluids to prevent overload. NSAIDs increase bleeding risk in thrombocytopenic patients.

blocks.heading: Evaluation
blocks.html: HCT decreased from 52% to 44%. Platelets increased to 85,000. BP 108/72, HR 88. Urine output 0.8 mL/kg/hr. No active bleeding. Entering recovery phase.
NRG Care Plan Formula: Problem → Goal → Interventions → Rationale → Evaluation

What system is being tested?

Multi-System / Environmental - vector-borne infection and organ involvement

What is the priority?

Fluid management (dengue critical phase) + species identification (malaria) + NO NSAIDs

What is unsafe?

Aspirin/NSAIDs in dengue, missing critical phase timing, no G6PD test before primaquine

What restores function?

Supportive care + fluid management allows recovery; ACT cures malaria; doxycycline for leptospirosis

blocks.heading: 💡 Key Memory Aids for RENR
blocks.html:
• NO NSAIDs in dengue: Aspirin/ibuprofen increase bleeding risk - acetaminophen ONLY
  • Critical phase timing: Days 3-7 during defervescence - plasma leakage and bleeding occur NOW
  • HCT rise = plasma leak: Hematocrit rising >20% with falling platelets = critical phase warning
  • Primaquine + G6PD: ALWAYS test G6PD before primaquine - causes hemolysis in deficiency
  • Species identification: ALWAYS identify malaria species - falciparum = emergency; vivax needs primaquine
NRG System Focus Formula: Vector-Borne Disease leads to Multi-System infection + endothelial damage causing Fluid leakage/hemolysis. Priority: Fluid management + species ID + NO NSAIDs

question.stem: A patient with confirmed dengue fever has a temperature of 38.5C and requests medication for fever relief. The platelet count is 55,000. Which medication should the nurse administer?

options.html: Aspirin 325 mg orally for its antipyretic and anti-inflammatory effects
Ibuprofen 400 mg orally to reduce fever and musculoskeletal pain
Acetaminophen 650 mg orally for fever reduction
Diclofenac 50 mg orally for pain and fever control

question.rationale: Dengue fever causes thrombocytopenia (platelets 55,000 in this case), which increases bleeding risk. NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac) all have antiplatelet effects and increase the risk of hemorrhage - they are CONTRAINDICATED in dengue. Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is the ONLY safe antipyretic/analgesic for dengue patients because it does not affect platelet function or increase bleeding risk. This is a standard nursing safety rule in dengue-endemic regions.

why.html: Aspirin is contraindicated in dengue - antiplatelet effect increases bleeding risk
Ibuprofen is an NSAID - contraindicated with thrombocytopenia
Diclofenac is an NSAID - increases bleeding risk in dengue
